phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ], palatal approximant [j], open-mid front vowel [ɛ], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥˥). Pinyin 'x' before front vowels is [ɕ], never English 'ks' or 'z'.

pronunciation.approximation: SHYEHN — a high, level tone held steady, with a light 'sh' that touches the palate.

kin.label: Classical Chinese
kin.form: Xiān, an immortal, transcendent, or perfected being.

kin.label: Related terms
kin.form: 神仙 shénxiān (god-immortal); 仙人 xiānrén (immortal person); 八仙 Bāxiān (Eight Immortals)

pronunciation.note: 仙 denotes a transcendent being in Daoism, distinct from ordinary gods (shén) and from Buddhist arhats or bodhisattvas. The character combines 人 (person) with 山 (mountain), suggesting one who withdraws to the heights. The Pinyin restoration Xiān preserves the high level tone.

domains.title: The Immortal
domains.subtitle: Transcendence, Daoist Practice, and Celestial Freedom
domains.lead:
Xiān is the Chinese immortal: a human being who has refined body and spirit until death no longer applies. Unlike the gods of popular religion, who receive offerings and grant petitions, the xiān has escaped the bureaucracy of heaven and earth. He or she dwells in mountains, rides clouds or cranes, and appears unpredictably to those who have cultivated the Dao.

The path to becoming xiān is not faith but practice: meditation, breath control, diet, alchemy, and moral discipline. Immortality is an achievement, not a gift.

cards.name: Longevity
cards.desc: The xiān has overcome ageing and death through disciplined transformation of the body.

cards.name: Mountain Dwelling
cards.desc: Immortals withdraw to peaks and grottoes where the qi is pure and the world is far.

cards.name: Internal Alchemy
cards.desc: Neidan refines the three treasures — jīng, qì, shén — into an immortal embryo.

cards.name: Freedom from Bureaucracy
cards.desc: Unlike gods bound by celestial office, the xiān wanders freely between realms.

symbols.name: Crane
symbols.meaning: The mount and companion of immortals; a thousand-year lifespan.

symbols.name: Peach of immortality
symbols.meaning: The fruit of the Queen Mother of the West's garden, ripening every three thousand years.

symbols.name: Gourd
symbols.meaning: The bottle that holds elixirs, medicines, and the boundless space of the Dao.

symbols.name: Clouds and mist
symbols.meaning: The medium through which immortals travel and the boundary between mortal and transcendent realms.

mythology.lead: Xiān mythology is a vast gallery of individual adepts, each with a distinctive method of transcendence — and a long argument, running from the Zhuāngzǐ to the Míng novel, about what exactly escapes when a human being escapes death.

myths.title: The Divine Person of Mount Gūshè
myths.text: The xiān blueprint is drawn before the word has fully settled. In the first chapter of the Zhuāngzǐ the philosopher describes the shénrén, the divine person of Mount Gūshè: skin like frost and snow, gentle as a maiden, who does not eat the five grains but sucks the wind and drinks the dew, mounts the clouds and mist, rides the flying dragon, and roams beyond the four seas (Zhuāngzǐ, ch. 1). Nothing here requires doctrine — no elixir, no scripture, no school. The figure simply is what perfect alignment with the Dào looks like from outside: weightless, unhurried, ungovernable. Later Daoism would attach the label xiān to precisely this silhouette and then spend two thousand years working out the mechanics of achieving it. The myth’s power lies in its refusal to explain itself: transcendence first appears in Chinese literature not as a promise but as a description, offered in passing, of a person the world cannot hold.

myths.title: The First Hagiographies
myths.text: The Hàn scholar Liú Xiàng — or the circle writing in his name — assembled the Lièxiàn zhuàn, Biographies of Exemplary Immortals: the tradition’s founding hagiography, some seventy lives of the transcendent. Its gallery is startlingly democratic. Chìsōngzǐ, Master Redpine, rain-master to the god-king Shénnóng, who entered the fire and ascended; Wángzi Qiáo, the crown prince who abandoned his throne to play the shēng mouth-organ on a mountain, and who was last seen riding a white crane skyward; woodcutters, courtiers, silkworm-tenders — each perfected by an idiosyncratic path (Lièxiàn zhuàn, Hàn dynasty). The collection fixed the genre’s grammar — birth omen, eccentric practice, wondrous departure — that every later Daoist hagiography would reuse. Its quiet revolution was sociological: the gods had always taken offerings, but immortality, it turned out, could be earned by almost anyone, including people history would otherwise never have recorded.

myths.title: The Pharmacology of Gold
myths.text: The fourth-century alchemist Gé Hóng gave transcendence a laboratory. In the Bāpōu zǐ, ‘Master Who Embraces Simplicity,’ he grades the achievement: the highest adepts rise bodily into heaven; middling ones roam the mountains as earthly immortals; the lowest attain liberation by shedding the corpse — and all three ranks are earned through elixirs compounded from cinnabar, gold, mica, and jade (Gé Hóng, Bāpōu zǐ, Nèipiān ch. 2). The logic is explicit in the text: he who takes gold lives as long as gold. The programme was lethal as often as liberating — mercury poisoning claimed many a sincere adept — but its audacity is the point: immortality treated not as grace but as technology, with recipes, dosages, and quality control. Chinese alchemy never split from its sacred purpose; the furnace was an altar, and the elixir a sacrament you could get wrong.

myths.title: Liberation from the Corpse
myths.text: The strangest road to heaven leaves a body behind. Shījié, ‘liberation from the corpse,’ is the rite of the substituted body: the adept appears to die and is buried with full honours, while the corpse in the coffin — revealed later to be a sword, a staff, or a bamboo tube — was never flesh at all (Gé Hóng, Bāpōu zǐ, Nèipiān ch. 2; cases recorded in Táo Hóngjǐng’s Zhēngāo). Gé Hóng ranks it frankly as the lowest grade of transcendence, and the medieval church catalogued its abuses — charlatans seeding tombs with props to gull the grieving. Yet the motif solves a real theological knot: if the Dào transforms the whole person, what happens to the body the villagers watched grow old? The answer is a decoy. The tomb is left as evidence for those who need evidence, and the xiān walks out of his own funeral into a lifespan measured in centuries — the only exit from mortality that requires, first, a convincing death.

myths.title: The Eight Immortals Cross the Sea
myths.text: The most beloved xiān are a team, and a late one. The Eight Immortals — Lǚ Dòngbīn the scholar, Zhōnglí Quán the general, Zhāng Guǒlǎo on his mule, Hé Xiāngū the maiden, Lán Cǎihé of ambiguous gender, Hán Xiāngzǐ, Cáo Guójiù, and Lǐ Tiěguǎi the lame beggar with an iron crutch — crystallised as a set only in the Yuán and Míng, after the Táng cataloguer Dù Guāngtíng had already gathered the raw material in his Yǒngchéng jíxiān lù (10th c.). Their signature episode is the crossing of the sea: forbidden the clouds, each crosses by throwing a personal token into the waves — a flower-basket, a gourd, castanets — and riding it across, giving Chinese its proverb ‘the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each showing their divine skill’ (Míng novel Dōngyóu jì). The myth’s message is the team’s composition itself: transcendence is not a caste but a trade guild, open to beggars, soldiers, and courtiers alike, provided each brings one impossible skill.

lore.syncretism: The xiān tradition absorbed many influences. Indigenous Chinese quest for longevity merged with shamanic flight, alchemical experimentation, and Buddhist meditation techniques. The figure of the wandering immortal influenced Chan Buddhism, Confucian self-cultivation, and Chinese poetry and painting. In popular religion, local spirits and historical figures were posthumously enrolled as xiān. The West knows the xiān chiefly through the Eight Immortals and martial-arts films, where they appear as eccentric sages with superhuman powers. Modern Daoist lineages continue to practice neidan in pursuit of the same goal.
lore.culturalLegacy: Xiān permeate Chinese culture. They appear in landscape painting as tiny figures on misty peaks, in New Year prints carrying peaches and gourds, and in countless novels, operas, and films. The aspiration to longevity shapes Chinese medicine, diet, and exercise practices such as tai chi and qigong. The word xiān is also used for extraordinary people: a great cook is a 'food immortal,' a beautiful woman a 'fairy.' In global spirituality, the xiān offers an alternative to Western heaven: not a reward after death but a transformation of life itself, achieved through sustained practice.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Xiān is the promise that the human body is not a prison. Unlike religions that split soul from flesh, Daoist immortality aims to refine the body until it becomes light, durable, and free. The xiān does not escape the world; the world loses its grip.

This is a demanding hope. It requires decades of breath, diet, meditation, and moral care. It asks whether we are willing to treat our own embodiment as a craft rather than a given. The immortal on the crane is not a tourist in transcendence but an artisan of spirit. To name a domain Xiān is to claim that the highest human possibility is not power or knowledge but freedom — the freedom that comes from having made oneself compatible with the Dao.

lore.archaeology: The xiān tradition is attested in Warring States and Han dynasty texts, tomb art showing feathered immortals ascending to heaven, and the Mawangdui tomb manuscripts on longevity and breath cultivation. Medieval Daoist caves and temple murals depict the Eight Immortals and other transcendent figures. Alchemists' stoves, elixir recipes, and neidan manuals survive in the Daozang and in archaeological contexts from the Han through the Song dynasties.
